name: jolie
why: A service-oriented language where programs are microservices and communication is first-class, a genuinely different way to think about code.

brief.what_it_is: Jolie is a programming language for building systems out of services. Per the homepage, the basic building blocks are services that can be relocated and replicated as needed, and a composition of services is itself a service. Jolie is contract-first: types and interfaces (for example requestResponse and oneWay operations) are declared up front, and the interpreter handles data transformations between types. The homepage's sample takes a JSON HTTP request with a name field and returns a greeting string. The brew package ships a set of executables, including jolie, joliec, joliedoc, joliemock, metaservice, and converters such as wsdl2jolie, openapi2jolie, jolie2java, and jolie2wsdl; those names come from the package metadata, not from the homepage.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Jolie as a way to make the concepts of service-oriented computing into linguistic constructs, so that the building blocks of software are services rather than objects or functions. It is pitched at microservices and APIs, and at keeping a monolith's logic unchanged while it is split across machines.
brief.how_it_works: A Jolie program is a service with input ports (location, protocol, interfaces) and a main block that handles operations. The same logic can run locally or remotely, and one program can be exposed over several protocols at once (the homepage shows HTTP/JSON, SOAP, and a binary protocol called SODEP on separate ports). Native operators express workflow: the homepage example 'login( credentials )() { checkCredentials }; { publish( x ) | edit( y ) }' uses ';' for sequence and '|' for parallel. Fault handling uses scope and install so handlers can be changed at runtime. Java and JavaScript code can be embedded, and new protocols can be added through a Java API.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no installation steps. Its Download page is linked from the navigation, but both guessed paths (download.html and download) returned 404, so I could not verify the install process, runtime requirements, or first-run steps. The homepage links to a tutorial titled 'Get Started Now' for a first project, which I did not reach.
brief.standout: Jolie makes the service itself the unit of code: the same program can move from local to remote or be split across machines without changing its logic, and a composition of services is again a service you can expose. The language also has built-in sequence and parallel operators and runtime-updatable fault handlers for parallel code, which is not common in mainstream languages.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows a copyright range of 2014-2024 and a News section, but I found no release date, commit date, or maintenance note on the pages I could read.
brief.caveats: I could not reach the Download or Docs pages, so platform support, install steps, and build requirements are unverified. The homepage claims formal semantics and use in research and teaching but gives no details. Licensing: the website text is CC BY 4.0 and the code samples are GPL v2, per the footer; the language's own license was not stated on the homepage. The brief's executable list comes from package metadata, not from documentation I read. The homepage's 'Vision' and 'About' pages were not fetched.
quotes: Jolie crystallises the programming concepts of service-oriented computing as linguistic constructs.
The basic building blocks of software are not objects or functions, but rather services that can be relocated and replicated as needed. A composition of services is a service.
Jolie is a contract-first programming language, which puts API design at the forefront.
Jolie is protocol agnostic: your services can exchange data by using different protocols.

judge.reason: Jolie makes services, protocol boundaries, and parallel composition language-level constructs, offering a genuinely different way to model and relocate software.

entry.title: Jolie
entry.tldr: A programming language where the basic unit is a service, not an object or function, so one program can run locally, remotely, or over several protocols at once.
entry.deeper_look:
Jolie is a language for building systems out of services. A program is a service with input ports (a location, a protocol, and interfaces) and a main block that handles operations. Its homepage puts the premise this way: "The basic building blocks of software are not objects or functions, but rather services that can be relocated and replicated as needed. A composition of services is a service."

It is contract-first. You declare types and interfaces up front, with operations such as requestResponse and oneWay, and the interpreter handles data transformation between types. The same logic can be exposed over several protocols on separate ports. The homepage shows HTTP/JSON, SOAP, and a binary protocol called SODEP. Its sample takes a JSON HTTP request with a name field and returns a greeting string.

Workflow is built into the syntax. The homepage example `login( credentials )() { checkCredentials }; { publish( x ) | edit( y ) }` uses `;` for sequence and `|` for parallel. Fault handling uses scope and install, so handlers can be changed at runtime. Java and JavaScript can be embedded, and new protocols can be added through a Java API.

The idea underneath is that microservice concerns like communication, protocols, and composition become language constructs instead of framework glue. The homepage also pitches it for splitting a monolith across machines without changing its logic. The brew package ships a toolbox beyond the interpreter, including converters such as wsdl2jolie, openapi2jolie, jolie2java, and jolie2wsdl, plus joliedoc and joliemock.
entry.install:
brew install jolie
# pulls in openjdk as a dependency; Jolie runs on the Java runtime

try_this.what_happens: Lists the interpreter's options, a safe first look before you write any service.
Shows how to generate documentation from a service's interfaces.
Shows the options for the mock tool, which comes with the package.

entry.whats_unique: Services, ports, protocols, and parallel composition are part of the language itself, not a framework on top. One program can be served over HTTP/JSON, SOAP, and a binary protocol simultaneously.
entry.caveats: I could not reach the download or docs pages, so install steps and maintenance status are unverified. The homepage shows a 2014-2024 copyright range but no release dates.
